questions.stem: What is the main aim of green chemistry?

options.text: To make chemicals cheaper to produce
To stop all chemical manufacturing
To design chemical processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances and minimise environmental impact
To make all chemicals green in colour

questions.explanation: Green chemistry aims to design chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and generation of hazardous substances, minimising the impact on human health and the environment.

questions.stem: What does 'atom economy' mean in green chemistry?

options.text: The cost of each atom used in a reaction
The percentage of atoms in the reactants that end up in the desired product
The speed at which atoms react
The number of atoms in a molecule

questions.explanation: Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that are incorporated into the desired product. A high atom economy means less waste is produced, which is a key principle of green chemistry.

questions.stem: Why is using a catalyst considered a green chemistry approach?

options.text: Because catalysts reduce the energy needed for reactions, lower temperatures required, and can be reused
Because catalysts are only made from natural materials
Because catalysts make products more colourful
Because catalysts are always green in colour

questions.explanation: Catalysts lower the activation energy needed for reactions, meaning lower temperatures and pressures can be used. This saves energy, reduces costs, and decreases environmental impact. Catalysts are also not consumed and can be reused.

questions.stem: Which type of solvent is preferred in green chemistry?

options.text: Water or other non-toxic, renewable solvents
Toxic organic solvents
Solvents made from crude oil only
Concentrated acids

questions.explanation: Green chemistry favours using water or other non-toxic, renewable solvents instead of harmful organic solvents. This reduces the risk to workers and the environment, and avoids generating hazardous waste.

questions.stem: How does using renewable feedstocks support green chemistry?

options.text: They produce more waste than non-renewable feedstocks
Renewable feedstocks are always cheaper
They are only used in the food industry
They reduce dependence on finite resources like crude oil and can be replenished naturally

questions.explanation: Using renewable feedstocks (such as plant-based materials instead of petrochemicals) reduces dependence on finite fossil fuel reserves and supports sustainability, as these materials can be regrown.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of designing chemical products that are biodegradable?

options.text: They are more expensive to dispose of
They are always stronger than non-biodegradable products
They break down naturally in the environment, reducing long-term pollution
They last forever in landfill

questions.explanation: Biodegradable products can be broken down by microorganisms in the environment into harmless substances. This reduces the accumulation of persistent pollutants and waste in landfill and the natural environment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of green chemistry in practice?

options.text: Using excess reactants to ensure a high yield
Disposing of chemical waste in a river
Developing a process that uses a catalyst, water as a solvent, and produces minimal waste
Using the highest possible temperature for all reactions

questions.explanation: A process that uses a catalyst (reducing energy), water as a solvent (non-toxic), and produces minimal waste (high atom economy) exemplifies multiple green chemistry principles working together.
